17274: This is a rare passage where worshippers of another god speak for themselves. Two readings of the same history collide: the people think disaster came because they abandoned the goddess; the prophet says it came because they served her. The book sides with Jeremiah but records the argument honestly.
17275: Who was the Queen of Heaven?
17276: Candidates include Ishtar (whose title in Akkadian was 'Lady of Heaven' and who received star-shaped cakes), Astarte, Anat (called 'lady of heaven' in Egypt), or Asherah. Many scholars think Judahite worship blended features of several goddesses. The identity is debated.
17278: Scholars such as Susan Ackerman stress that this was family worship, led by women, alongside temple religion. It shows that the prophets' 'Yahweh alone' faith was not yet everyone's practice.
17279: A link with the Elephantine Jews?
17280: A Jewish colony in Egypt a century later swore by 'Anat-Yahu', which some see as a continuation of this goddess worship among Egyptian Jews. The connection is possible but unproven.
17282: Later Christians called Mary 'Queen of Heaven'. Some Protestant writers have linked the two; Catholic and Orthodox writers reply that the Marian title grew from Christian reflection on Christ's kingship and has no historical connection with the goddess of Jer 44. Historians agree there is no direct line between them.
17283: Isaiah's idol satire and the bowing of Bel and Nebo
17285: Those who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit; their witnesses neither see nor know.
17287: The smith works with his strong arm, grows hungry and faint, and drinks no water: the god-maker is weaker than he thinks.
17289: The carpenter measures out a human figure; he plants a cedar, and the rain makes it grow (rain that comes from Yahweh, not the idol).
17290: Half for dinner, half for a god
17291: With half the log he roasts meat and warms himself; with the rest he makes a god, bows down and prays, 'Save me, for you are my god'.
17293: No one says, 'Shall I fall down before a block of wood?' He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray.
17295: Bel (Marduk) and Nebo (Nabu), the great gods of Babylon carried in its New Year procession, are pictured as heavy loads on weary animals, unable to save themselves, going into captivity.
17297: By contrast Yahweh has carried Israel from birth and will carry them to old age. People carry their idols; this God carries his people.
17298: A scarecrow in a cucumber field
17299: Jeremiah uses the same satire: idols are like scarecrows that cannot speak and must be carried. One verse in Jeremiah is even written in Aramaic, the language of the empire, as a message to the nations.
17300: In exile the question was whether Babylon's gods had defeated Israel's. These chapters answer with mockery: the idols are man-made, must be carried, and cannot act, whereas Yahweh made the heavens, controls history and carries his people. Here the Bible moves closest to saying that the other gods are not real at all.
17302: Most scholars date Isa 40-55 to the late exile (c. 550-539 BC), when Cyrus was rising and Babylon's gods were close at hand; the satire fits that setting.
17304: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers, and some modern conservative scholars, hold that the 8th-century Isaiah wrote these chapters prophetically, which makes the naming of Cyrus (Isa 44:28; Isa 45:1) predictive.
17306: Babylonian theologians did not think the wood was the god: a ritual of 'washing the mouth' was believed to make the image a dwelling of the deity. Critics call Isaiah's account a caricature; defenders reply that satire deliberately exposes the material base of the practice, and that ordinary worshippers did treat images as the god.
17308: Cyrus took Babylon peacefully in 539 BC and honoured Marduk (see the Cyrus Cylinder). Some read Isa 46 as theological poetry rather than a forecast; others point to later damage under Xerxes, or see the 'bowing' fulfilled in Babylon's fall from power.
17309: Paul among the gods: Lystra, Athens and Ephesus
17312: At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth.
17314: The crowd shouts in Lycaonian that the gods have come down in human form, calling Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, 'because he was the chief speaker'.
17316: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood before the city, brings oxen and garlands to sacrifice to them.
17318: Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes and urge them to turn from 'these vain things' to the living God who gives rain and fruitful seasons. Soon after, the crowd turns and stones Paul.
17320: In Athens Paul is provoked by a city full of idols and debates in the synagogue and the marketplace.
17322: Before the Areopagus he points to an altar 'to an unknown god' and announces that God as the Creator who does not live in shrines made by hands.
17324: Quoting Greek poets, Paul argues that humans are God's offspring, so God cannot be like gold or stone, and calls all people to repent because of the coming judgment by the risen man.
17326: In Ephesus the silversmith Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, warns that Paul's preaching that 'gods made with hands are not gods' threatens both trade and the goddess. A crowd shouts her praise for two hours in the theatre.
17327: The town clerk calms the crowd
17328: The town clerk reminds them that Ephesus is guardian of Artemis and of the image that fell from heaven, notes that Paul's group were neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers, and dismisses the assembly.
17329: The old contest continues in the Greek world, but the weapons change. There is no fire from heaven: Paul refuses worship, reasons from creation, adapts to his audience, and the gods lose ground through conversion and economics rather than by force.
17331: The Roman poet Ovid tells of Zeus (Jupiter) and Hermes (Mercury) visiting a Phrygian couple, Philemon and Baucis, in disguise, and punishing those who refused them hospitality (*Metamorphoses* 8). Many commentators think a local version of this story explains the crowd's eagerness not to miss a divine visit.
17333: Many read Acts 17 as a model of meeting people where they are: using their altar and their poets to point to the Creator. Others stress that the speech ends in a sharp call to repentance and a resurrection that most hearers mocked.
17335: Paul's letters hold two thoughts together: an idol is nothing and there is one God (1 Cor 8:4-6), yet pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Cor 10:19-21). Acts shows the public face of the first thought.
17337: Details such as the Lycaonian language, the 'temple-warden' title of Ephesus and the town clerk's office fit local inscriptions, which many take as signs of good information; others think Luke shaped the speeches freely, as ancient historians did.
17338: Probably 'man of Baal' or 'Baal exists'. In Saul's day 'baal' (lord) may simply have been a title for Israel's own God.
17342: Chronicles keeps the older form of the name of Saul's son, while Samuel uses the 'shame' form. A name 'Eshbaal son of Beda' was found on a jar from Khirbet Qeiyafa (published 2015), showing the name was in real use around 1000 BC. Hosea 2:16-17 shows why: by the 8th century prophets wanted 'Baal' removed from Israel's vocabulary altogether, even as a title for Yahweh.
17343: Uncertain: perhaps 'Baal is my advocate' or 'hero of Baal'.
17345: Uncertain; usually taken as 'from the mouth of shame' or 'one who scatters shame'. The key element is 'bosheth', shame.
17346: Substitution of 'bosheth' for 'baal', with a reshaped first element.
17347: Jonathan's lame son appears as Merib-baal in Chronicles and as Mephibosheth in Samuel. Saul's son by Rizpah, also called Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8), probably had a Baal-name originally too. The exact meaning of both forms is uncertain, but the swap of 'baal' for 'bosheth' is widely accepted.
17348: Probably 'may Baal contend' or 'Baal founds/increases'. Judges explains it as 'let Baal contend against him', because Gideon tore down Baal's altar.
17352: Gideon's other name keeps 'Baal' throughout Judges, but in 2 Sam 11:21 (Joab's message to David) it becomes Jerubbesheth. Judges 6:32 is itself a pun turning a pro-Baal name into a taunt against Baal; most scholars think the original name was a normal Baal-honouring name.
17353: 'Baal knows' (or 'the Lord knows', if baal is a title).
17357: A son of David born in Jerusalem. Here the pattern is reversed from Saul's family: Chronicles 14:7 keeps Beeliada, while Samuel and the other list in Chronicles use Eliada. It shows that even David gave a son a Baal-name, almost certainly meaning 'the Lord knows' with Yahweh in mind, and that later scribes found this uncomfortable.
17358: The name of the great West Semitic goddess of love and war, known in Phoenician inscriptions and in Greek as Astarte.
17359: The goddess's consonants read with the vowels of 'bosheth' (shame), so the reader says 'shame' while saying her name.
17360: Re-vocalisation: the consonants are kept, the vowels of bosheth are imposed.
17361: Hebrew was originally written without vowels, so later readers supplied them. Outside the Bible the goddess is Ashtart; only in the Hebrew Bible is she 'Ashtoreth'. The plural Ashtaroth (Judg 2:13) is used for the goddesses generally. A few scholars think the vocalisation could be a dialect form, but most accept the 'shame' pun.
17362: 'King'. Could be a divine title ('the King') or, on a Punic parallel, a technical term for a kind of sacrifice (molk).
17364: Re-vocalisation with the vowels of bosheth.
17365: The same consonants give Milcom, god of Ammon (1 Kgs 11:5; 1 Kgs 11:33), and 1 Kgs 11:7 calls the same Ammonite god 'Molech'. In 1935 Otto Eissfeldt argued from Punic inscriptions that 'to Molech' originally meant 'as a molk-offering', so no god Molech existed; many scholars followed him. Others (for example John Day and George Heider) argue for a real underworld god, pointing to a deity mlk in Ugaritic and Akkadian texts and to Lev 20:5, 'to go whoring after Molech'. Either way, the vowels of 'shame' seem deliberate.
17366: Probably 'Baal the Prince' or 'Lord of the exalted dwelling'. Ugaritic texts call Baal zbl b'l ars, 'Prince, Lord of the earth'.
17368: One-letter change turning a title of honour into a contemptuous nickname.
17369: Greek manuscripts of the Gospels have Beelzebul, which preserves the older 'prince/dwelling' form; the Latin Vulgate and the KJV have Beelzebub. Jesus' wordplay on 'the master of the house' (Matt 10:25) may play on zebul, 'dwelling'. A minority think Baal-zebub was a genuine title of a fly-averting healing god (Greek parallels like Zeus Apomyios, 'averter of flies'), so the pun is likely but not certain.
17370: The hill east of Jerusalem, called Mount of Anointing in later Jewish usage because of its olive oil.
17371: har ha-mashchit, 'Mount of Corruption' (or 'of the Destroyer')
17373: Near-homophone pun: a one-letter difference between 'anointing' and 'destruction'.
17374: Solomon's shrines for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom stood on this hill for about three centuries until Josiah defiled them. The pun is widely recognised, though the 'Mount of Anointing' name is attested only in later Jewish sources, and some take mashchit simply as a description ('the hill of destruction') with no wordplay intended.
17375: 'House of God (El)', the shrine where Jacob dreamed and where Jeroboam set up a golden calf.
17379: Hosea mocks the calf-shrine at Bethel as Beth-aven; Amos makes a similar pun ('Bethel shall come to nought', aven). A real place called Beth-aven near Ai existed (Josh 7:2), which Hosea may be exploiting; but in Hosea 10:5 the 'calf of Beth-aven' is plainly Bethel's calf.
17380: A normal Babylonian name honouring Nabu (biblical Nebo).
17382: No clear meaning; 'nego' is not a known god.
17383: Possible deliberate distortion of the god's name (bu changed to go), or ordinary sound change.
17384: Many scholars think 'nego' disguises 'Nabu', so that a faithful Jew is not called 'servant of Nabu'. Others think it is simply an Aramaic or scribal form and no insult is meant. Elsewhere the Bible names Nebo plainly (Isa 46:1), and Daniel's own Babylonian name, Belteshazzar, keeps Bel-related elements (Dan 4:8), so the change, if deliberate, was not systematic.
17385: Ashima was a deity brought to Samaria by settlers from Hamath.
17388: Sound-alike pun turning a god's name into 'guilt'.
17389: Amos condemns those who 'swear by the sin (ashmat) of Samaria'. Many translations (for example NRSV 'Ashimah of Samaria') take this as a veiled god-name. Since Amos predates the Assyrian resettlement of 2 Kgs 17, some prefer to see Asherah of Samaria (known from Kuntillet Ajrud) or a calf-cult behind it; others think 'guilt' is meant literally.
17390: Ordinary words for cult images and gods.
17392: Often explained as 'dung-idols' or 'dung-balls', from gel / galal, dung.
17393: Coined insult: idols named with a word that sounds like dung, vowelled like shiqqutsim, 'detestable things'.
17394: Ezekiel uses gillulim nearly 40 times; it is his favourite word for idols. The link with dung (compare Ezek 4:12) is widely held but not proven; some derive it from galal, 'to roll', meaning round stones or blocks. Either way it is a contemptuous word, not a neutral one.
17395: The normal word for gods (and also for Israel's God).
17398: Sound-alike pun on el/elohim using a word built on 'al (not, nothing).
17399: 'All the gods (elohim) of the peoples are nothings (elilim), but Yahweh made the heavens' (Ps 96:5). The Greek Septuagint translated elilim here as daimonia, 'demons', a key step in the later idea that the gods were demons.
17400: The god whose cult Antiochus IV installed in the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC, called Zeus Olympios in Greek sources.
17401: shiqquts shomem, 'the abomination that makes desolate'
17403: Double substitution: shiqquts (detestable thing) for 'baal', and shomem (desolating) as a pun on shamem (heaven).
17404: Proposed by Eberhard Nestle in 1884 and accepted by many commentators. The same word shiqquts replaces 'god' elsewhere: 1 Kgs 11:5 calls Milcom 'the abomination of the Ammonites', where 1 Kgs 11:33 says 'the god of the Ammonites'. Readers who take Daniel as predictive prophecy of a later desolation often accept the pun while reading the fulfilment differently.
17405: Ugarit (Ras Shamra) tablets and the Baal Cycle
17406: c. 1400-1185 BC (most myths copied in the 13th century BC)
17407: Ras Shamra and Minet el-Beida, near Latakia, Syria
17408: In 1928 a farmer's plough struck an ancient tomb at Minet el-Beida on the Syrian coast. French excavations under Claude Schaeffer began at nearby Ras Shamra in 1929 and found clay tablets in a previously unknown alphabetic cuneiform, deciphered within about a year (1930) by Hans Bauer, Edouard Dhorme and Charles Virolleaud. Among them is the Baal Cycle: Baal (Hadad), the storm god, defeats Yam (Sea) with clubs made by Kothar-wa-Khasis, gets a palace on Mount Zaphon, is swallowed by Mot (Death), and returns after his sister Anat destroys Mot. Other texts describe El, the aged father of the gods, his consort Athirat (Asherah) and the assembly of the 'sons of El'.
17409: Before Ugarit, Baal, Asherah and El were known mostly from the Bible's attacks on them. Ugarit let scholars hear Canaanite religion in its own words and revealed many shared images: Baal as 'rider of the clouds' (compare Ps 68:4), the seven-headed sea serpent Lotan (compare Leviathan, Isa 27:1), Zaphon as the holy mountain (Ps 48:2), El as an aged king (compare Dan 7:9) and a council of gods (Ps 82:1). Scholars debate whether the Bible borrows, adapts or polemicises against these motifs.
17411: Dhiban (biblical Dibon), Jordan; now in the Louvre, Paris
17412: In 1868 local Bedouin showed the missionary F. A. Klein a black basalt stone about 1 m high with 34 lines of writing. Prussian and French agents competed to acquire it; under Ottoman pressure, locals heated the stone and poured cold water on it, shattering it. Before that, Charles Clermont-Ganneau had obtained a paper squeeze (impression), torn while still wet; the text was reconstructed from the squeeze and about two-thirds of the fragments. Mesha says Omri of Israel oppressed Moab 'because Chemosh was angry with his land', that Chemosh told him to take Nebo, that he killed its 7,000 inhabitants and devoted them to Ashtar-Chemosh, and that he dragged the vessels of YHWH before Chemosh.
17413: It is the longest Iron Age inscription from the region, names Omri and Israel, and contains one of the earliest securely dated mentions of YHWH outside the Bible. It shows a neighbour using the same theology as Kings in reverse: a nation's god angry with his land, then giving victory, and 'devoting' a city to destruction (herem). A reading 'house of David' in line 31 has been proposed (André Lemaire) but is debated.
17414: Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions: 'Yahweh and his asherah'
17416: Excavated in 1975-76 by Ze'ev Meshel, this remote way-station on a desert route had storage jars (pithoi) and plastered walls with inscriptions and drawings. One jar reads, in essence, 'I bless you by YHWH of Samaria and by his asherah'; another invokes 'YHWH of Teman and his asherah'. Plaster texts mention El and Baal. Drawings include Bes-like figures and a seated lyre player, which some have identified as Yahweh and Asherah.
17417: The find shows that some Israelites around 800 BC blessed people in the name of Yahweh together with an 'asherah'. Grammar is the crux: Hebrew normally does not add 'his' to a personal name, so many read 'his asherah' as a cult object (a sacred pole or tree) associated with Yahweh; others argue it means the goddess as Yahweh's consort. Most scholars think the drawings and the inscriptions were not made as a single scene, so the 'Yahweh and Asherah' picture is doubtful.
17420: William Dever recovered this inscription from a looted Iron Age tomb in 1967. Carved roughly into a pillar above a downward-pointing hand, it reads something like: 'Uriyahu the rich wrote it. Blessed be Uriyahu by YHWH; from his enemies by his asherah he has saved him.' The letters are poorly cut and several readings are possible.
17421: It is a second, independent witness from Judah (not just the north) to blessing by 'YHWH and his asherah'. With Kuntillet Ajrud it is central to the debate over how widespread Asherah worship alongside Yahweh was in popular religion.
17422: Tel Arad shrine and the 2020 residue study
17423: c. 760-715 BC (shrine stratum); residue study published 2020
17425: Yohanan Aharoni's excavations (1962-67) uncovered a small shrine inside a Judahite royal fortress, with a niche holding at least one standing stone (massebah) and two limestone incense altars on its steps. In 2020 a team led by Eran Arie analysed residues on the altars: the larger held frankincense mixed with animal fat; the smaller held cannabis mixed with animal dung (used to keep it smouldering). The shrine was later deliberately covered over.
17426: It shows an official Judahite shrine outside Jerusalem, of the kind later reforms condemned (2 Kgs 18:4; 2 Kgs 23:8). The cannabis is the earliest known evidence of the drug in Judah and among the earliest in the Near East, suggesting mind-altering incense in worship. Whether the standing stones stood for Yahweh alone or Yahweh with a consort, and whether the shrine was buried under Hezekiah, Josiah or for other reasons, are debated.
17429: Found in 1996 in a large temple complex during excavations led by Seymour Gitin and Trude Dothan, this five-line stone inscription records a temple built by Ikausu (Achish) son of Padi, ruler of Ekron, for 'Ptgyh his lady', asking her to bless and protect him and prolong his days. Padi and Ikausu are both known as kings of Ekron in Assyrian records.
17430: It confirms Ekron's identification, gives a list of Philistine kings matching Assyrian sources, and names a goddess, Ptgyh, otherwise unknown; she may be an Aegean goddess (some suggest a form of Greek Potnia, 'lady'), reflecting the Philistines' origins. It is a reminder that the gods of Ekron were more varied than the single 'Baal-zebub' of 2 Kings 1. The name Achish also matches the Philistine king of Gath in Samuel.
17433: Found in 1921 and excavated repeatedly since (notably by Lawrence Stager's team in the 1970s), this Phoenician burial ground held thousands of urns, estimated at over 20,000 across its history, containing the burned bones of infants and young animals, under stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit. Some stelae use the word mlk for an offering. Greek and Roman writers (for example Diodorus Siculus, *Library* 20.14) describe Carthaginian child sacrifice, including a bronze statue from which children rolled into fire.
17434: The site is the main evidence for the 'molk' sacrifice behind the biblical Topheth and 'passing children through fire to Molech'. In 2010 a team led by Jeffrey Schwartz argued that many remains were prenatal or newborn, suggesting a cemetery for natural deaths; in 2011-2013 a team including Patricia Smith, correcting for shrinkage of burned bone, found ages clustered in the first weeks of life, consistent with sacrifice. Most scholars now accept that at least some children were sacrificed, but the scale and practice remain debated.
17437: Found in 1968 by Paul Lapp's expedition, this clay stand about 60 cm tall has four decorated tiers: a naked female figure between two lions; an empty space flanked by winged sphinxes (cherubim); a sacred tree with two ibexes flanked by lions; and at the top a young bull or horse beneath a winged sun disc.
17438: Many scholars read the female figure and the tree as representations of Asherah. The empty space between cherubim has been read as the invisible presence of Yahweh, and the animal under the sun disc as Yahweh (or Baal) linked with the sun, compare the 'horses of the sun' removed by Josiah. The stand suggests a combined iconography of Yahweh and Asherah in northern Israel, but each identification is debated.
17439: Tel Dan sacred precinct (high place and altar)
17441: Tel Dan, at the springs of the Jordan
17442: Avraham Biran's long excavation (from 1966) uncovered a sacred precinct with a large stone platform (bamah), the remains of a horned altar, smaller incense altars and iron shovels for handling ashes. A later bilingual Greek-Aramaic inscription (found 1976) reads 'To the god who is in Dan'. The 'house of David' stele found in 1993-94 came from the same site.
17443: Most scholars identify the platform with the royal sanctuary Jeroboam I founded and later kings enlarged, the site of one of the two golden calves. No calf has been found. It shows a major state shrine of the northern kingdom that rivalled Jerusalem for centuries.
17445: Babylon (Esagila, Marduk's temple area); now in the British Museum
17446: Found by Hormuzd Rassam in 1879, this clay barrel records Cyrus of Persia's capture of Babylon. It says Marduk was angry with the last king, Nabonidus, searched for a righteous ruler, called Cyrus by name and let him enter Babylon without battle. Cyrus claims to have returned gods to their sanctuaries and gathered their peoples back to their homes.
